CST201.start: If you can read a small C program, start with branches and loops, then reuse those ideas on arrays. If syntax is new, use Unit 1 as a short warm-up and return to this order.

1.title: Read a short C expression
1.reason: These short expression traces and header explanations make a useful third pass. If syntax is the thing slowing you down, do this unit as a warm-up.
essentials: Operator precedence and assignment versus comparison
Headers, common types and conversions
1.try: Predict the results of 5/2 and 5/2.0, then trace one expression that mixes multiplication and addition. Explain where parentheses would change the result.

examples.task: Predict the result of an expression that mixes division, multiplication and addition.
Explain precedence, associativity and the difference between a header and a library.

recall: Integer division discards the fractional part; 5 / 2 is 2.
Precedence groups operators; associativity breaks ties within a precedence level.

patterns.title: Operator precedence and output tracing
patterns.prompt: Add parentheses to show how an expression is evaluated. Explain precedence and associativity, then predict the output of a short expression.

patterns.title: Header files and their purpose
patterns.prompt: Explain why a header is included, distinguish it from a library file, and name a relevant standard header in a short example.

patterns.title: Type conversion and integer division
patterns.prompt: Explain a cast or predict what happens to a value when the operands or the receiving type change. Check integer division separately.

patterns.title: Bitwise operators
patterns.prompt: Define bitwise operations and show one with a short bit pattern.

2.title: Trace the branch and the loop
2.reason: Short loop templates cover written comparisons and full programs. The same dry run helps with both the running-total series and GCD.
essentials: Trace while and do–while before coding
Rehearse one branch problem and one running-total loop
2.try: Trace digit sum with input 402, noting each remainder and updated value. Then write a GCD loop and test it with 18 and 12.

examples.task: Write the running-total series using loops.
Compare while and do–while, then write a GCD program.

recall: while tests before the body; do–while tests afterward.
In a nested loop, show where the inner counter and any running total are reset.

patterns.title: Compare loop types
patterns.prompt: Show when each loop tests its condition. Give an example where while and do–while behave differently.

patterns.title: Switch–case or nested if–else
patterns.prompt: Write a small branching program and explain when switch–case is a good fit. Be ready to draw the nested-if flow.

patterns.title: Sum a series of running totals
patterns.prompt: Given n, write a program to add 1, then 1 + 2, then 1 + 2 + 3, and so on. Trace your accumulator on a small input.

patterns.title: Explain loop control statements
patterns.prompt: Trace what break or continue changes, and explain why an unstructured jump can make the program harder to follow.

patterns.title: Find the GCD of two numbers
patterns.prompt: Write a loop for Euclid’s algorithm. Show how each remainder becomes the next divisor, and state when the loop stops.

3.title: Work through arrays and strings
3.reason: Matrix and string questions reuse loops you already know. A clear index trace is useful across several written question forms.
essentials: Matrix rows, columns, diagonals and transpose
String terminator and basic library functions
3.try: Sketch a 3 × 3 matrix, mark its diagonal indices, and write a loop that adds only those elements. Then draw how a short string is stored.

examples.task: Sum the diagonal of a 4 × 4 matrix.
Show string functions and check an input string for a palindrome.

recall: In a square matrix the main diagonal has row index equal to column index.
A C string needs room for the terminating null character as well as its visible characters.

patterns.title: Matrix programs
patterns.prompt: Write nested loops for a task such as finding diagonal elements, checking an identity matrix, or producing a transpose. Label rows and columns.

patterns.title: String library functions
patterns.prompt: Explain or implement the requested string operation: copy, concatenate, compare or find length. Give an input and the expected result.

patterns.title: Process a string character by character
patterns.prompt: Practise a manual string operation such as reversal, case conversion or a palindrome check. Show the indices you compare or advance.

patterns.title: Array declarations and subscripts
patterns.prompt: Declare a one-dimensional array, give an initializer and check which subscripts are valid. Explain why the last index is one less than the length.

4.title: Turn a solution into a function
4.reason: Storage-class comparisons and parameter examples are reusable. Recursion is worth practising after you can trace the same task with a loop.
essentials: Prototype, call and return value
Compare scopes and trace a recursive base case
4.try: Write a factorial function and trace the stack by hand for input 3. Test the base case separately.

examples.task: Compare storage classes and passing a value versus an address.
Write a recursive factorial function.

recall: Scope is where a name is visible; lifetime is how long the object exists.
C passes arguments by value. A copy of an address still lets the function access the original object.

patterns.title: Storage classes and scope
patterns.prompt: Explain the common storage classes with small declarations. Compare scope, lifetime and the behaviour of repeated calls.

patterns.title: Passing arguments by value or address
patterns.prompt: Use one small example to show why passing a value does not change the caller’s variable but using its address can.

patterns.title: Function declaration and parameters
patterns.prompt: Distinguish a prototype or declaration from a definition. Label actual and formal parameters in an example call.

patterns.title: Recursive functions
patterns.prompt: Write a base case and show the call sequence for a numeric example. Be able to compare the recursive and iterative versions.

5.title: Draw pointers before writing code
5.reason: Pointers turn up in written questions, but correct traversal and allocation take more careful tracing. Start them after arrays and function calls.
essentials: Draw address, pointer and value separately
Trace allocation, failure check, use and cleanup
5.try: Draw a small dynamically allocated array. Write the allocation, failure check, traversal and cleanup in that order.

examples.task: Explain address-of and dereference, then access an array using pointers.
Explain malloc, calloc, realloc and free.

recall: For a valid index i, a[i] is equivalent to *(a + i).
Check whether allocation succeeded before dereferencing, and release owned memory when done.

patterns.title: Pointer declarations and dereferencing
patterns.prompt: Show a valid declaration and label the address-of and dereference operations. Explain what the pointer refers to.

patterns.title: Array access with pointers
patterns.prompt: Traverse an array or find an element through a pointer. Relate pointer arithmetic to the element type and the array indices.

patterns.title: Dynamic allocation routines
patterns.prompt: Compare malloc, calloc, realloc and free. In a program, show where allocation is checked and where memory is released.

patterns.title: Pointer to a function
patterns.prompt: Explain what a pointer to a function refers to, and sketch a declaration and a call using it.

checklist: Trace one loop on a normal input and a boundary case.
Explain the index bounds of a matrix and the terminator of a C string.
Identify the return value and base case of a recursive function.
Draw what a pointer refers to and say where allocated memory is freed.

CST203.topics: Python basics, functions, files and Django
CST203.start: Start with short loop and condition problems you can dry-run on paper. Next revise collections, then functions. A Django flow diagram is a quicker first pass than learning several file and regular-expression APIs at once.

1.title: Choose a type and predict the result
1.reason: Comparing collections and dry-running slices are short tasks with both objective and written examples in the archive.
essentials: Lists versus tuples and dictionaries
Index, slice, split and join on small examples
1.try: Make a list of five values. Predict two slices and try changing an element; explain how the same operation differs on a tuple.

examples.task: Compare lists, tuples and dictionaries, and distinguish indexing from slicing.
Show what join and split do and explain string immutability.

recall: Indexing normally selects one element; a slice excludes its stop index.
split separates a string into a list; separator.join combines strings into one.

patterns.title: Lists, tuples and dictionaries
patterns.prompt: Compare how lists, tuples and dictionaries store and change values. Give a short example and identify which examples are mutable.

patterns.title: Indexing and slicing
patterns.prompt: Predict which elements a slice selects. Explain the difference between a slice and an index using a small list.

patterns.title: String methods and formatting
patterns.prompt: Show what split and join return. Practise a string-formatting example and explain why changing one character does not mutate a string.

patterns.title: Data types and conversions
patterns.prompt: Identify built-in types in examples and show how to convert a number or string. Explain when the interpreter converts a value and when an explicit conversion is needed.

patterns.title: Membership, identity and other operators
patterns.prompt: Demonstrate an operator with a short expression and explain the result. In particular, distinguish membership, equality and identity.

2.title: Dry-run conditions and loops
2.reason: Loop traces and small programs appear repeatedly. One dry-run habit transfers to range, prime checks and break/continue questions.
essentials: for, while and range with a dry run
if–elif–else and break versus continue
2.try: Write a prime checker and dry-run it on 1, 2 and 9. Mark exactly which condition rejects a composite number.

examples.task: Explain break, continue and pass, then write a prime checker.
Compare for and while and write a digit-sum program.

recall: range(start, stop) excludes stop; check the first and last loop values.
break exits the loop, continue advances to the next iteration, and pass does nothing.

patterns.title: Trace loops and range
patterns.prompt: Compare for and while, then predict the values a small range-based loop prints. Identify the update and the stopping condition.

patterns.title: Break, continue and pass
patterns.prompt: On the same loop input, show which iteration is skipped or which statement ends the loop. Distinguish pass from both.

patterns.title: Check whether a value is a palindrome
patterns.prompt: Write a short program for the numeric or string version in the paper. Check a palindrome, a non-palindrome and a one-character case.

patterns.title: Test whether a number is prime
patterns.prompt: Write a divisibility loop. Test it with 1, 2 and a composite number, and explain when the loop can stop.

patterns.title: Indentation and conditional branching
patterns.prompt: Mark the statements inside and outside an indented branch, then show which branch runs on two inputs.

3.title: Package small, testable functions
3.reason: Function-argument and scope questions reuse a few compact examples. Practise those before writing longer scripts or following imports.
essentials: Default and variable-length arguments
Local/global scope and module versus package
3.try: Write a function with one default argument, call it with and without that argument, and move it to a module that you import.

examples.task: Give examples of positional, default and variable-length arguments.
Compare module and package, and distinguish local, global and nonlocal scope.

recall: An argument is the value supplied at a call; a parameter is the name in the definition.
A package groups modules. Test an import with the same directory layout you describe.

patterns.title: Function arguments and return
patterns.prompt: Demonstrate positional, default, keyword or variable-length arguments. Use a small call and state what is returned.

patterns.title: Scope of variables
patterns.prompt: Show which names are available inside and outside a function. Distinguish local, global and nonlocal scope using an example.

patterns.title: Modules, packages and imports
patterns.prompt: Compare a module with a package, draw a tiny package layout and give a valid import statement.

patterns.title: Lambda functions
patterns.prompt: Explain a lambda with a one-expression example. State its inputs and result, and compare with an ordinary named function.

4.title: Read a file and extract a match
4.reason: File questions are useful, but modes, read/write methods and regex returns need separate practice. Learn them after the short reusable answers.
essentials: Choose the file mode before any operation
Compare readline, readlines, match and findall
4.try: Read a short text file, count its lines, and use a regular expression to pick out digit groups from the text.

examples.task: Explain file access modes and show read and write methods.
Compare re.match, re.split and re.findall with examples.

recall: In text mode, r reads, w truncates or creates, and a appends or creates.
re.match checks from the start of the string; re.search can find a match later.

patterns.title: Choose a file mode
patterns.prompt: Explain what happens when opening an existing or missing file in the requested mode. Use a separate example for reading, writing and appending.

patterns.title: Read and write methods
patterns.prompt: Compare the file methods by the data they return or accept. Demonstrate read, readline, readlines, write and writelines where relevant.

patterns.title: Work with a text file
patterns.prompt: Practise an open–read–process–close solution. For a word count, explain how the text is split and counted; for output, state what is written.

patterns.title: Regular-expression matching
patterns.prompt: Explain pattern matching and compare methods such as match, split and findall on one short test string.

5.title: Follow a Django request
5.reason: Start with the repeatable architecture diagram and template purpose. Project setup and forms can follow as separate practice.
essentials: Map URL → view → template
Know what templates and static files are used for
5.try: Draw the route for a page that lists books, labelling what receives the URL and what displays the list. Add where a form would be validated.

examples.task: Describe Django’s MVC/MTV architecture.
Show how to insert a static file into a Django template.

recall: A URL pattern selects a view; a view can render a template with context data.
A template controls presentation; CSS and images are static assets, not template context.

patterns.title: Explain MVC and Django’s MTV architecture
patterns.prompt: Label the responsibilities in a diagram. Describe how the model, template and view work together for a page request.

patterns.title: Templates and static assets
patterns.prompt: Explain why a template is used for page output and how static files can be referenced or managed.

patterns.title: What Django is and when to use it
patterns.prompt: Describe why a web app might use Django. When comparing with Flask, state your project assumptions instead of claiming one is always better.

patterns.title: Create and run a Django project
patterns.prompt: Outline the setup and run steps. Practise explaining the difference between a project and an app as you walk through the process.

checklist: Predict a slice and the output of a loop before you run either.
Show a call with a default argument and explain what the function returns.
Pick a file mode and a regular-expression method for a small task.
Sketch a Django URL, view and template flow without looking at the notes.

CST205.topics: Stacks, queues, linked lists, trees and graphs
CST205.start: Start with stack and queue traces, then draw linked-list operations step by step. If classification words are unfamiliar, skim the Unit 1 definitions first. Leave the longer tree and graph traces for a separate pass.

1.title: Name the structure and its operations
1.reason: The definitions are fast to revise, but most of the practice here is comparing and explaining. Put the reusable stack and linked-list algorithms first unless the terms are unfamiliar.
essentials: Linear versus non-linear structure with examples
Basic operations and abstract data type
1.try: Pick a linear structure and a non-linear one. Sketch both and describe what it means to visit every element in each.

examples.task: Define a data structure and compare linear with non-linear structures.
Give an example of an abstract data type.

recall: An ADT describes operations and behaviour, not the underlying storage layout.
A sequence is linear; a tree is non-linear because a node can branch.

patterns.title: Linear and non-linear structures
patterns.prompt: Classify examples by how their elements relate. Give a clear difference with a linear and a non-linear example.

patterns.title: Primitive types and structures
patterns.prompt: Define primitive and non-primitive structures and distinguish a data type from a data structure using an example.

patterns.title: Abstract data type
patterns.prompt: Define an ADT and give an example. Describe its operations before choosing how to implement them.

patterns.title: Common operations and their preconditions
patterns.prompt: Explain insertion, deletion and traversal. Discuss what happens if insertion is attempted without spare capacity.

2.title: Trace stacks and circular queues
2.reason: Push/pop, postfix and circular queues recur in full questions. One trace table helps with algorithms, boundary cases and objective items.
essentials: Write stack operations and evaluate postfix
Trace front and rear in a circular queue
2.try: Evaluate the postfix expression 8 3 − 2 × with a stack. Then use a circular capacity of four and trace rear as it wraps after a dequeue.

examples.task: Write push and pop algorithms with overflow and underflow checks.
Write circular-queue insertion and deletion algorithms.

recall: A stack is last-in, first-out. For a binary operator in postfix, the first pop is its right operand.
A circular queue wraps an index using modulo capacity. State how your version distinguishes full from empty.

patterns.title: Stack push, pop and boundary cases
patterns.prompt: Write the array-based push and pop algorithms. Trace the top index, including full and empty cases.

patterns.title: Infix and postfix exercises
patterns.prompt: Use a stack to convert or evaluate the expression requested in the paper. Record the stack state after each token.

patterns.title: Circular queue operations
patterns.prompt: Trace insertion and deletion with a front and rear. Show when each index wraps and explain how full and empty are distinguished.

patterns.title: Deque and restricted operations
patterns.prompt: Draw the two ends of a deque and distinguish input-restricted from output-restricted operations.

patterns.title: Recursive problem solving
patterns.prompt: Identify the base case and show smaller calls in a GCD or Tower of Hanoi solution. Compare recursion with iteration.

3.title: Draw before and after each list operation
3.reason: Insertion and comparison questions reuse a before/after diagram. Practise singly linked lists first, then add back links or a circular tail.
essentials: Insert and delete at the head, tail and middle
Draw singly, doubly and circular variants
3.try: On paper, insert into an empty list, insert in the middle, and delete the last node. Label which references change each time.

examples.task: Insert a node at the beginning of a singly linked list.
Compare a linked list with an array and describe the advantage of back links.

recall: In a singly linked insertion, save the old successor before replacing its link.
In a circular list, stop on returning to the starting node, not on finding NULL.

patterns.title: Insert into a singly linked list
patterns.prompt: Write an insertion algorithm and sketch the affected links. Trace the separate cases for the beginning, middle and end of the list.

patterns.title: Array versus linked list
patterns.prompt: Compare storage and access, then give a case where you would choose each representation.

patterns.title: Doubly linked-list behaviour
patterns.prompt: Label previous and next links, explain the benefit of two-way traversal and show which references are updated.

patterns.title: Circular linked lists
patterns.prompt: Draw a circular linked list, explain the last link and distinguish it from a list that terminates with NULL.

patterns.title: Represent a polynomial as a linked list
patterns.prompt: Draw a node layout for a polynomial term and show how links connect the terms of the given expression.

4.title: Separate tree and graph traces
4.reason: Trees and graph traversals have good past-paper coverage, but they need several distinct traces. Give AVL, traversal and graph work separate time.
essentials: Reconstruct trees and practise AVL rotations
Trace BFS/DFS with a named start vertex
4.try: Take a small tree and write all three traversal orders. On a small graph, run BFS and DFS from the same vertex and compare the orders.

examples.task: Reconstruct the tree from in-order and pre-order and give post-order.
Explain AVL rotations and construct an AVL tree from the given values.

recall: With distinct keys, the first pre-order item is the root; in-order separates the subtrees.
BFS uses a queue. DFS can use a stack or recursion. Mark visited vertices when tracing a graph.

patterns.title: Tree traversals and reconstruction
patterns.prompt: Use the given in-order and pre-order lists to reconstruct the tree. Check the result by producing another traversal.

patterns.title: AVL trees and rotations
patterns.prompt: Insert values one at a time, identify the imbalance and show the rotation after which the tree is balanced.

patterns.title: B-tree properties and construction
patterns.prompt: Explain the properties of a B-tree of a given order. For an insertion trace, draw the node split and the promoted key.

patterns.title: Graph representation
patterns.prompt: Draw a small graph and give its adjacency matrix or adjacency list. Explain why the chosen representation suits it.

patterns.title: Graph traversal with BFS and DFS
patterns.prompt: Practise BFS with a queue, then compare it with DFS. Specify the start vertex and neighbour order, and show how you track visited vertices.

checklist: Check empty and full conditions in a stack or queue trace.
Draw a linked-list insertion and label the updated links.
Redo a tree traversal and an AVL rotation without notes.
State the starting vertex and neighbour order when tracing a graph.

CST207.start: Start with the 8086 diagram and addressing modes. You can reuse the same labelled drawings and a few short operand examples. If the hardware vocabulary is new, skim the Unit 1 computer diagram before that first pass.

1.title: Draw the path that data takes
1.reason: A labelled computer diagram and a short register trace are easy to rehearse. Do the floating-point exercises as a second pass within this unit.
essentials: Von Neumann functional units and buses
Register shifts, two’s complement and bit fields
1.try: Draw the Von Neumann block diagram without notes, then encode −6 with eight bits using two’s complement. Check which bits change in a logical right shift.

examples.task: Draw the Von Neumann blocks and explain the buses.
Compare fixed-point and floating-point formats, then encode −75 in eight bits.

recall: Address, data and control buses carry different kinds of signals; label all three.
IEEE binary32 has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits.

patterns.title: Von Neumann architecture and buses
patterns.prompt: Draw a labelled computer diagram and show how instructions and data reach the CPU. Explain what each bus carries.

patterns.title: Floating-point representation
patterns.prompt: Label the sign, exponent and fraction fields of an IEEE representation. When asked, compare fixed-point and floating-point formats.

patterns.title: Two’s complement representation
patterns.prompt: Write the requested negative number using the stated bit width, and show the intermediate steps.

patterns.title: Register micro-operations and shifts
patterns.prompt: Identify a register micro-operation and trace a shift on a small register value. State which bits enter and leave the register.

2.title: Trace arithmetic, control and the pipeline
2.reason: This unit has substantial written examples, but arithmetic traces, control sequencing and hazards are separate skills. Tackle them once the shorter diagrams are secure.
essentials: Control memory and instruction pipeline
Booth multiplication and restoring division traces
2.try: Trace a small signed multiplication using the taught register format. Draw a separate pipeline timeline and mark where a dependency can delay an instruction.

examples.task: Explain pipelining and identify the kinds of hazards.
Multiply two negative numbers using Booth’s algorithm.

recall: An arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit; a logical right shift fills with zero.
A pipeline can improve throughput without reducing the latency of one instruction.

patterns.title: Pipelining and hazards
patterns.prompt: Draw the stages and identify a hazard on a short timeline. Explain how a mitigation changes the execution.

patterns.title: Microprogrammed control
patterns.prompt: Draw the control-memory path and explain address sequencing. Compare with hardwired control when the paper asks for it.

patterns.title: Signed multiplication with Booth’s algorithm
patterns.prompt: Track the registers for the given operands. State the bit width and show each add/subtract/shift decision.

patterns.title: Restoring division
patterns.prompt: Show the subtract, test and restore steps for a small unsigned example. Label the quotient and remainder.

patterns.title: Vector processing
patterns.prompt: Explain what a vector instruction does to a collection of elements. Give one example and distinguish it from a scalar operation.

3.title: Label the 8086 before memorising instructions
3.reason: Addressing-mode questions recur and the architecture uses repeatable diagrams. Rehearse one example per mode before studying all pin details.
essentials: 8086 blocks, BIU, EU and registers
Addressing modes with one instruction each
3.try: Draw the BIU and EU and label several registers. Explain which part of each example instruction tells you where its operand comes from.

examples.task: Explain 8086 addressing modes with examples.
Explain the 8086 internal architecture and describe interrupt types.

recall: The BIU handles bus transfers and instruction fetch; the EU executes instructions.
For a memory operand, distinguish the offset from the physical address formed using the segment.

patterns.title: Addressing modes and 8086 examples
patterns.prompt: Name the addressing mode from an instruction and explain how its operand or address is obtained. Give several short examples.

patterns.title: 8086 internal architecture
patterns.prompt: Draw the BIU and EU, label the registers and describe how instruction fetching and execution are coordinated.

patterns.title: Minimum and maximum modes
patterns.prompt: Compare minimum and maximum modes and identify the purpose of the mode selection or relevant pins in the diagram.

patterns.title: Types of interrupts
patterns.prompt: Distinguish maskable and non-maskable interrupts. Sketch how an interrupt transfers control to a service routine.

4.title: Track the state after each instruction
4.reason: A short register trace is a good first drill, but the archived examples here are less consistent than those for 8086 addressing or cache. Use the notes for branches, procedures and macros as well.
essentials: Trace data movement and register arithmetic
Distinguish a normal call from an interrupt
4.try: Write a short sequence that adds two register values and stores the result elsewhere. Trace what each instruction changes before adding a branch.

examples.task: Choose an assembly sequence that adds two registers and saves the result.
Write zero-address instructions to evaluate an arithmetic expression.

recall: For 8086 Intel syntax, MOV destination, source copies the value into the destination.
Keep a register table. Add a row after each instruction that changes a register or flag.

patterns.title: Data movement instructions
patterns.prompt: Identify what changes after a data transfer: which operand is read and which register or location receives the value. Use the instruction set in the paper.

patterns.title: Register arithmetic and result storage
patterns.prompt: Trace an arithmetic instruction or write a short register-based addition sequence using the notation in the paper.

patterns.title: Stack-based instructions for expressions
patterns.prompt: Translate an expression into zero-address operations and trace the intermediate values. This is a stack-machine exercise, not native 8086 syntax.

patterns.title: Calls and interrupts
patterns.prompt: Compare a subroutine call with an interrupt service routine. Identify what initiates each transfer of control.

patterns.title: Input/output instructions
patterns.prompt: Identify the instructions used for port input and output, and explain the direction of each transfer.

5.title: Keep cache, virtual memory and interfacing separate
5.reason: Mapping comparisons and hit-ratio questions reuse similar worked examples. Add memory interfacing after you can distinguish cache and address translation.
essentials: Cache mappings and hit/miss calculations
Virtual memory, TLB and where an address goes
5.try: Sketch a direct-mapped cache lookup, then draw a separate RAM/ROM address-selection example from the notes.

examples.task: Explain the cache mappings and calculate average access time.
Explain direct mapping and define virtual memory.

recall: Direct mapping assigns a block to one cache line; a set-associative cache offers ways within a set.
For average access time, distinguish the time of a hit from the total time of a miss.

patterns.title: Cache mapping
patterns.prompt: Compare direct, associative and set-associative mapping. Use a small address example to explain a direct-mapped cache.

patterns.title: Hit ratio and effective access time
patterns.prompt: Explain hit and miss ratio, then use the access times and assumptions in the question to set up the calculation.

patterns.title: Virtual memory and address translation
patterns.prompt: Explain virtual memory and the TLB. Where asked, distinguish virtual addresses from physical memory or cache mapping.

patterns.title: Memory chip organisation and interfacing
patterns.prompt: Sketch how the processor selects RAM or ROM/EPROM. Check capacity from the number of locations and the bits stored per location.

checklist: Draw the computer blocks and explain what moves along each bus.
Label the 8086 BIU and EU, and identify an instruction’s addressing mode.
Show the intermediate register values in an arithmetic or assembly trace.
Explain a pipeline hazard, a cache lookup and address translation as three separate ideas.

CST209.start: Begin with binary search and hashing; both are quick to demonstrate on a small input. Next practise sorting passes. Read Unit 1 notation first only if you cannot yet label the time or space cost of a trace.

1.title: Count work before naming the growth rate
1.reason: The definitions are quick, but search and sort traces give you more chances to practise a complete procedure. If you get stuck on the notation, use this unit as a warm-up.
essentials: Properties of an algorithm and common bounds
Distinguish time, space and the case being analysed
1.try: Count iterations for a loop that increments by one and one that doubles its index. Show your reasoning for both before writing the asymptotic bound.

examples.task: Explain algorithm characteristics and common asymptotic notations.
Count iterations in a loop whose index doubles.

recall: O gives an upper bound; Ω gives a lower bound; Θ gives a tight bound.
Name what n measures and whether you are counting time or auxiliary space.

patterns.title: Define a good algorithm
patterns.prompt: Define an algorithm and explain its characteristics with a small example or a counterexample.

patterns.title: Big O, Omega and Theta
patterns.prompt: Explain the bounds with an example. Distinguish a tight bound from an upper or lower bound.

patterns.title: Time and space complexity
patterns.prompt: Identify the input size and count the key operation in a short loop. Distinguish that cost from the extra memory used.

patterns.title: Divide and conquer
patterns.prompt: Explain the split, solve and combine steps. Compare with dynamic programming or identify the design model used in a known algorithm.

patterns.title: Sets and multisets
patterns.prompt: Explain how a set and multiset differ using a collection that contains the same value twice.

2.title: Show the intermediate sorting passes
2.reason: Simple sorts are quick to trace and frequently tested. Start with one array and reuse it before moving to pivot selection and non-comparison methods.
essentials: Write one pass each for bubble, selection and insertion
Compare merge/quick/heap sorts, then practise radix
2.try: Trace selection sort and merge sort on the same short list with a duplicate value. Write the array after each pass or merge.

examples.task: Write bubble sort and show the array after each pass.
Trace selection sort and state its worst-case time complexity.

recall: Selection sort picks a minimum; insertion sort puts the next item into a sorted prefix.
State the pivot and partition rule before tracing quicksort.

patterns.title: Bubble sort passes
patterns.prompt: Write the bubble sort steps and trace the array after each pass. State when the version you use can stop.

patterns.title: Selection sort
patterns.prompt: Trace which minimum is selected in each pass. State what the sorted prefix contains after each swap and give the worst-case time bound.

patterns.title: Insertion sort
patterns.prompt: Trace the shifting and insertion steps as each new item is inserted into a sorted prefix. Compare the work for sorted and reverse-sorted input.

patterns.title: Merge sort and comparison-sort costs
patterns.prompt: Show the split and merge steps. Compare merge, quick and heap sort on time and extra space when requested.

patterns.title: Quick sort and partitioning
patterns.prompt: Show how the pivot partitions the input. Explain how different partitions affect best- and worst-case costs.

patterns.title: Linear-time sorts
patterns.prompt: Explain what makes a non-comparison sort applicable. Trace bucket or radix sorting on the given input.

3.title: State the search assumptions
3.reason: Binary search and hash collisions have repeatable traces in written groups. Start with those before practising more involved tree updates.
essentials: Binary search with a missing key and sorted input
One hash collision and a BST insertion/deletion
3.try: Find a present key and an absent key with binary search. Then place two keys in a small hash table so you can demonstrate one collision.

examples.task: Write recursive binary search and explain why the input must be sorted.
Explain hashing and compare collision-resolution techniques.

recall: Binary search discards half of a sorted search interval at each comparison.
Chaining stores colliding keys in a bucket; probing searches for another slot.

patterns.title: Binary search and when to use it
patterns.prompt: Write binary search and show how the bounds change. State when linear search is appropriate and what binary search assumes.

patterns.title: Hashing and collision resolution
patterns.prompt: Explain the hash function and trace one collision. Show chaining or the probing procedure requested in the paper.

patterns.title: Binary search tree operations
patterns.prompt: Sketch a BST built from the input order. Trace an insert or delete and show how the ordering invariant is preserved.

patterns.title: Height-balanced search trees
patterns.prompt: Explain why height balancing matters for search. Practise identifying the balance factor or the effect of a rotation.

4.title: Choose the graph algorithm for the goal
4.reason: Graph questions provide written practice, but shortest paths, minimum spanning trees and topological order solve different problems. Keep a separate trace for each.
essentials: Prim versus Kruskal on the same graph
Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford, Floyd–Warshall and DAG order
4.try: Run Prim’s and Dijkstra’s algorithms on the same small undirected graph with positive weights. Record each chosen edge or updated distance and explain the different goals.

examples.task: Explain and trace Prim’s algorithm for a minimum spanning tree.
Write Dijkstra’s algorithm and demonstrate the distance updates.

recall: A minimum spanning tree minimizes total tree weight, not distance from a source.
Dijkstra needs non-negative edge weights. A topological order requires a directed acyclic graph.

patterns.title: Minimum spanning trees with Prim or Kruskal
patterns.prompt: Construct a spanning tree on the given weighted graph. Show the order in which edges are chosen and when an edge is rejected.

patterns.title: Dijkstra’s shortest paths
patterns.prompt: Trace distance updates from one source. State the required edge-weight assumption and show the final distances.

patterns.title: Bellman–Ford and negative weights
patterns.prompt: Show how the supplied edges are relaxed over repeated passes and explain when the algorithm is appropriate.

patterns.title: Floyd–Warshall and all-pairs paths
patterns.prompt: Set up the distance matrix for a small graph and show how considering an additional intermediate vertex changes it.

patterns.title: Directed acyclic graphs and topological order
patterns.prompt: Recognise a DAG and explain how a topological order respects dependencies. Draw examples with and without a cycle.

checklist: Name the input size and case before writing a time bound.
Show passes for a sort, and test a binary search with an absent key.
Trace a BST update or a hash collision without notes.
Name the graph goal and edge assumptions before starting the trace.
